newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire rebels target Kinshasa, diamond capital.
newsitem.headline: Zaire rebels target Kinshasa, diamond capital.

text.p: Zairean rebel leader Laurent Kabila declared a ceasefire around the captured city of Kisangani on Tuesday and said Kinshasa and a diamond centre were the next targets.
The Congolese Red Cross meanwhile said members of ailing President Mobutu Sese Seko's family had joined Zaireans taking refuge in neighbouring Congo in the face of rebel advances.
At rebel headquarters in the eastern border city of Goma, Kabila said he was declaring a temporary ceasefire for 20 km (13 miles) around Kisangani to allow in aid and let people return.

"We will not go to Ubundu while the ceasefire at Kisangani holds if they (Zairean troops) do not attack us," Kabila told a news conference. Some 100,000 refugees fleeing the rebels are massed around Ubundu, 100 km (60 miles) southeast of Kisangani.
Addressing more than 10,000 supporters in Goma on Tuesday, Kabila said the next rebel targets were the capital Kinshasa and diamond-mining capital of Mbuju-Mayi in central Kasai region.
He said rebels were pushing deeper into Kasai and had thrust 113 km (70 miles) west of the Zaire river, which runs through Kisangani. He said rebel forces could reach Kinshasa by June.
He added his forces were within 400 km (250 miles) of Mbuji-Mayi and Zairean troops had fled there from Kisangani.
"They will flee from there as they have fled before, what can they do to protect something which cannot be protected, we hear they are already laying down their arms," he said.
"We want to liberate Kinshasa and the people there need us."
In Kisangani, hundreds of Kabila's supporters paraded in triumph at the weekend capture of Zaire's third largest city.
"I want change, we want change. We are against the dictator and we welcome the rebels because we were in great trouble. Now we have been liberated," student Gorde Mabeja, 20, told Reuters.
Kisangani fell after a four-day battle north of the city against troops backed by Serb mercenaries, who fled an airport base last Friday following a reign of terror, residents said.
With rumours of an army coup rife in Kinshasa, Mobutu's son said on Tuesday the president was able to walk unaided in his hospital room in Monaco and planned to return home to try to stop the rebels.
He said the Mobutu, 66 and in power for 32 years, rejected any talks with Kabila. The president was admitted to hospital in Monte Carlo for treatement of prostate cancer on Sunday.

Ida Victorine Nze, president of the Congolese Red Cross, gave no details of which Mobutu family members arrived in Congo but said they left Kinshasa on Monday fearing things could take a turn for the worse.
Zairean Prime Minister Kengo wa Dondo arrived on Tuesday in Nairobi for talks and said that those seeking power in Africa's third largest country should do so by the ballot, not bullet.
Ending a Zairean government boycott of two previous rounds of talks in Nairobi on the crisis, Kengo said he wished Kenya's president success in his efforts to bring peace to Zaire.

"Power should be taken through votes and not by violence," Kengo said. "Those who are saying they can transform Zaire should make an appointment for elections that will take place under the supervision of the international community."
Kabila, whose fighters have seized more than 20 percent of Zaire since October, said even if he was invited to the Nairobi talks he would not have gone as Moi was a friend of Mobutu.
France, which has backed Mobutu, renewed its appeals on Tuesday to the rebels to agree to a ceasefire. A senior U.S. official visited Paris for talks on how to defuse the crisis.
